item.title: From the Zebra Puzzle to Murder Mystery Grids: How Deductive Cases Work
item.description:
Somebody slides a printout across the table. Five houses in a row, five nationalities, five drinks, five brands of cigarette, five pets. “Einstein wrote this,” they tell you. “Only two percent of people can solve it.” You draw five columns on a napkin, label them House 1 to House 5, and forty minutes later you know who owns the zebra.

Einstein didn’t write it. Nobody has turned up evidence for the two percent either. But the puzzle is real, and the same structure (a handful of categories, every item matched to exactly one item in each other category, a list of true clues) sits under every murder mystery logic grid you’ll find today. The napkin method doesn’t carry over, though, and the reason why explains the strange staircase-shaped chart that murder mysteries use instead.
